claims.text: The baseline alloy is equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo.
Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo forms a disordered BCC solid solution.
Equiatomic NbZrTiHfMo has a room-temperature compressive yield strength of approximately 1719 MPa.
High Mo content increases the electronegativity difference in NbZrTiHfMo.
The high Mo-associated electronegativity difference is detrimental to room-temperature plasticity.
Replacing one quarter of the Mo sublattice with V produces NbZrTiHf(Mo0.75V0.25), corresponding to approximately Nb20Zr20Ti20Hf20Mo15V5 in atomic percent.
V incorporation at this level reduces the alloy's electronegativity difference.
Partial replacement of Mo by V creates a modified lattice-distortion state.
The modified lattice-distortion state softens interatomic or elastic interactions.
The proposed V substitution preserves a single-phase disordered BCC solid solution.
Reducing the electronegativity difference decreases interatomic bonding strength.
Decreased interatomic bonding strength enables easier activation of slip systems.
Easier slip activation enhances dislocation mobility and compressive plasticity.
Strengthening from the refractory BCC matrix is retained after V substitution.
The modified alloy will retain a compressive yield strength near 1700 MPa and within approximately 5% of the baseline.
The modified alloy will show a 20–30% relative increase in room-temperature compressive plastic strain.
The beneficial strength-plasticity effect is limited to a narrow composition window in which the disordered BCC phase is retained.
Larger composition deviations may destabilize the phase constitution.
Larger composition deviations may compromise strength.
Controlled conventional arc melting and casting will ensure formation of the desired single-phase BCC alloy.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis predicts both retained strength and increased plastic strain, but the falsification rule requires both targets to fail simultaneously. Failure of either individual prediction should challenge the corresponding conjunct, yet under the stated rule it would not falsify the hypothesis.
